generalizedRange: Society Islands of French Polynesia — Moorea for this species; sister species on Tahiti and Huahine
hook: Every released snail wears a glowing dot. Then they found one without.

story.text: A Partula snail is a centimetre or two of coiled shell under a leaf in a Polynesian valley, feeding at night on rotting plant matter.
A hermaphrodite, it bears a single live young, a millimetre or two long, every few weeks.
In 1974 the rosy wolfsnail, a Florida carnivore, was released to control the giant African land snail — a control no rigorous evidence supports.
It preferred the tiny Partula; by 1995 almost every wild population was gone, and 52 species were extinct in the wild.
In the early 1990s conservationists gathered the last of 15 species and subspecies and carried them to zoos.
Releases began in 2015; each snail goes back with a dot of UV-reflective paint that glows under a torch at night.
In September 2024, on Moorea, surveyors found Partula tohiveana with no paint — four adults and thirteen juveniles, born wild, the first in 40 years.
The species moved from Extinct in the Wild to Critically Endangered, the first invertebrate to make that return.
Nearly 40,000 snails have gone home in a decade; by late 2025 wild-born tohiveana had spread beyond the release site.
To witness the Partula snail is to learn that a species can be held in a zoo for forty years, then handed back — one glowing dot at a time.

stats.size: Shell 0.5–1.2 in · 12–30 mm — most about the size of a fingernail
stats.lifespan: Up to 17 years in some species

reproduction.text: A hermaphrodite that gives birth to live young — one newborn a millimetre or two long every few weeks, after a gestation of about three months, and mature itself within three to six months.

insight.text: Every zoo-bred snail goes home wearing a dot of UV-reflective paint, so the proof that Partula tohiveana was truly back was finding snails with no dot at all.

programs.title: International Partula conservation breeding programme
programs.summary: Edinburgh Zoo has bred Partula snails since 1984 within the ZSL-coordinated collaboration of 15 zoos holding 15 species and subspecies, and has helped release more than 24,000 marked snails onto French Polynesian islands since 2015.

programs.title: Partula Species Survival Plan
programs.summary: Since 1990 the Saint Louis Zoo has coordinated the U.S. Partula Species Survival Plan, pooling snails bred at American zoos — more than 3,200 Partula nodosa in 2024 alone — and flying them to Tahiti for each year's release.
